records.place: Near Vicuña, Elqui Valley, Coquimbo, Chile

wine.name: Reserva Syrah
wine.grapes: Syrah alone, by the house's own sheet.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards in the Elqui Valley, the dry northern valley of the Coquimbo region where vines drink from the river, among them parcels around Vicuña on the old bed of the Elqui.
wine.making: Picked by hand into small boxes, destemmed and crushed, then fermented in stainless steel at a cool 22 to 24 degrees Celsius and taken through its malolactic fermentation. The wine is then aged in French oak barriques for some months, eight in the 2018 vintage by its importers' sheets, before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackberry and plum over black pepper, black olive tapenade and violet, with a smoky, meaty edge; ripe and full in the mouth but held by fresh acidity, with firm, fine tannin.
wine.ageing: Open and generous within two or three years of the vintage, it keeps its pepper and fruit for six to eight years from a good vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour if you like; a large Syrah or Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Used here for the house's barrique aged Syrah, a step above its plainest wines.
Chile's northern valley of the Coquimbo region, long known for pisco grapes before fine wine.

records.table: Viña Falernia's Reserva Syrah comes from the Elqui, Chile's northern valley of pisco grapes and clear skies. It smells of blackberry, black pepper and olive tapenade, with fresh acidity under the ripe fruit, so pour it beside grilled lamb.
records.story: The Elqui was pisco country long before it was wine country: a narrow, dry valley climbing from La Serena into the Andes, planted for brandy and table grapes. The family behind Falernia came to Chile from the Alpine village of Dimaro in the Trentino in 1951, by the accounts of its importers and guides, and in the early 1970s one of them settled at El Tambo, near Vicuña, to grow pisco grapes and later to distil. In 1998 he and a cousin, a winemaker from the Trentino, founded Viña Falernia to see whether the valley could make wine rather than spirit, and the cousin has made the wines from the start. The Syrah, grown on vineyards around Vicuña and further down the valley, proved the point: peppery, fresh and ripe at once, it gave the valley a wine name abroad. The house later added a second Elqui label, Mayu, and single vineyard Syrah from its Titón vineyard nearer the coast. For a sommelier the Reserva Syrah is where the far north of Chilean wine begins: a valley of sun tempered by altitude and the cold Pacific, and a Syrah that tastes of it.

others.name: Titón Single Vineyard Reserva Syrah
others.note: A Syrah from one block of the house's Titón vineyard, nearer the Pacific, aged in French oak.

others.name: Mayu

questions.exp: Falernia grows its Syrah in the Elqui, Chile's northern pisco valley near Vicuña; Colchagua is far to the south and warmer, and holds no part of this wine.

questions.q: Before Viña Falernia was founded in 1998, what did its founding family grow and make at El Tambo?
questions.exp: The family planted pisco grapes at El Tambo in the early 1970s and later distilled; wine came with Falernia in 1998.

report: The house's own site gave only a product page (Syrah alone, picked by hand into small boxes); its history page could not be read, so 1998, the family's arrival from Dimaro in 1951 and the pisco grapes of the early 1970s rest on Profile Wine Group and South America Wine Guide, which differ on 1971, 1972 and 1975 for the planting, hence the early 1970s.

The plan leaves the label open; the Reserva Syrah is chosen because it is the Syrah critics and merchants have listed across many vintages (Decanter, wine.com from 2006, a wine writer's site for 2010 and 2011); the Gran Reserva and Titón go in others.

The eight months in barrique is the 2018 sheet of Enotria and Coe and a UK merchant; the Gran Reserva 2021 sheet gives only part of the wine in barrel for six months, so the making is told by vintage.
The glass rests on Decanter's 2010 note (tapenade, black pepper, dark fruit) and a wine writer's 2011 note (black olive tapenade, violets, bacon fat).
Both founders are living and are described, not named.

Left out for want of a second source: the trophy said to have been won by the first Syrah in 2005, the claim of the first winery of the valley, the distillery's size and the Titón vineyard's altitude and distance from the sea, which the sources give differently.
The Titón vineyard nearer the coast is told only as relative; one source gives about 18 kilometres from the sea and another an altitude of 510 metres, so no figure is kept.

records.place: Alcohuaz, upper Elqui Valley, Coquimbo, Chile

wine.name: Tococo
wine.grapes: Syrah, alone in some vintages and with a little Petite Sirah in others.
wine.sites: A single vineyard planted in 2009 at about 1,788 metres in the upper Elqui, on sandy, decomposed granite of the Andes strewn with boulders.
wine.making: Whole bunches are fermented with their own wild yeasts in stone lagares, trodden by foot and with short macerations, and pressed in the old way. The wine is then aged about twenty months, eighteen to twenty two by vintage, in large wooden foudres of 2,500 litres.
wine.glass: Black plum, blueberry and blackberry over cracked pepper, olive tapenade and a flinty note of crushed granite; taut and fresh, with fine, well defined tannin.
wine.ageing: Tight when young and more open after five years or so; it should keep for well over a decade.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a large Syrah glass.

label.means: The single vineyard Syrah of the house, named after a bird of the valley.
Chile's northern valley of the Coquimbo region, here near its head in the Andes.

records.table: Tococo is the single vineyard Syrah of Viñedos de Alcohuaz, grown on granite at about 1,800 metres in the upper Elqui and trodden by foot in stone lagares. It is peppery, flinty and fresh, so give it time and air.
records.story: Alcohuaz is a hamlet near the head of the Elqui, where the valley narrows into the Andes and the slopes are boulders and sandy granite. A family from Santiago planted vines there from 2005, by the house's account, after a visiting friend suggested that the stony ground looked right for the vine; the father conceived the project and his son gave it its shape, with people born and raised in the valley beside them. The vineyards run from about 1,650 metres to over 2,200, high even for the Andes valleys of Chile. Rhu, a Syrah led blend from several parcels, was the first wine, with the 2011 vintage. The cellar works in the old way: short macerations, wild yeasts and stone lagares in which the grapes are trodden and pressed by foot, then long ageing in large foudres rather than small barrels. Tococo came from a single parcel planted in 2009 at about 1,788 metres and named after a bird of the valley, and it is the house's purest reading of Syrah on granite. To a sommelier it shows what altitude, rather than the sea, does in Chile's north: sun and cold nights, and a Syrah of tension and stone.

Alcohuaz is in the upper Elqui near the Andes, not in the coastal Limarí with its limestone and fog.

report: Founded 2005 rests on the house's own page (the La Era vines planted in 2005) and the importers' profiles (European Cellars, Vinoscout), which date the family's planting to 2005.
The founders, father and son, are living and are described, not named; so is the house's winemaker.
The ageing is told as about twenty months because the house's sheets give 18 (2021), 20 (2015) and 22 (2022) months in 2,500 litre foudres; European Cellars gives 23.
The blend moves by vintage: Syrah alone in 2022 by the house, 85 to 15 with Petite Sirah in 2020 and 2021 by the house and a wine writer's site.

The region record's line of vineyards above 2,000 metres is true of the estate's highest parcels but not of Tococo, which sits at about 1,788 metres; the region's producers line is otherwise borne out by the house's own account of treading and pressing by foot.

The glass draws on Wine Review Online's notes on the 2015 and 2019 vintages and the house's own note of granite stone in the 2022; the ageing window is a sommelier's estimate from those notes, so the checker may wish to soften it.
Left out: the founding family's names, and any first vintage of Tococo, which no source read gives.
The lint notes highest on the house's range of heights; the house's own figures are kept and the claim of the highest in Chile is not made.

records.place: Near Ovalle, Limarí Valley, Coquimbo, Chile

wine.name: Talinay Chardonnay
wine.sites: The Talinay vineyard, about 12 kilometres from the Pacific at some 150 metres, beside the Fray Jorge reserve, on porous, fractured limestone of an ancient marine terrace lifted to the surface, under the morning fog.
wine.making: Picked by hand into small boxes of 20 kilos, the grapes are fermented and aged in French oak barrels of several forests, Fontainebleau, Jupille and the Vosges among them, for ten or eleven months by the house's sheets for the 2022, with the lees stirred, before bottling.
wine.glass: Lime zest, green apple and crunchy pear over wet chalk and crushed seashells, with a salty, maritime edge and a faint nuttiness from the oak; linear and racy, with a long, fresh finish.
wine.ageing: Bright and taut on release, it gains texture over three to five years and should keep for eight or so.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The coastal vineyard of the house, on marine limestone near the Fray Jorge reserve.
The valley of the Coquimbo region around Ovalle, cooled by the Pacific and its morning fog.

records.table: Tabalí's Talinay Chardonnay grows on old marine limestone about 12 kilometres from the Pacific in the Limarí. It tastes of lime zest, green apple and wet chalk with a salty edge, so pour it cool with oysters or ceviche.
records.story: Tabalí takes its name from the old Hacienda Santa Rosa de Tabalí, in the Limarí Valley west of Ovalle, beside the Valle del Encanto, whose rocks carry petroglyphs of the El Molle people. A Chilean businessman of the Luksic family bought the hacienda in the early 1990s and planted its first vineyards in 1993, by the house's own account. The first Tabalí wines reached the market in 2002, and in 2004 the house built its modern cellar. The decisive step came in 2009, when, after years of geological study, Tabalí acquired the Talinay vineyard: a raised terrace of marine limestone about 12 kilometres from the sea, rare ground in Chile, beside the Fray Jorge reserve and under the morning fog the Chileans call camanchaca. Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc from Talinay became the wines the house is known by, and a parcel with more lime yet gives the Talinay Caliza. To a sommelier the Talinay Chardonnay is the Limarí's case in a glass: a desert valley turned cool by the Pacific, and limestone giving Chilean Chardonnay a chalky, saline cut.

report: Founded is left empty: the house's own page gives the purchase of the hacienda in the early 1990s, the first vines in 1993 and the first wines in 2002, and other sources say founded in 2002, so no one year is the founding; the plan's 2002 is the first wines.
The buyer of the hacienda died in 2013 by common report, but his dates were not read in two sources here, so he is described as a businessman of the Luksic family, not named.
The house's English sheet gives ten months in barrel and its Spanish sheet eleven for the 2022, so the making says ten or eleven.
The house's 2004 cellar is told without rank; several guides call it the first modern winery of the Limarí, a first claim left out.
The region record's producers line says Talinay defined the valley's Chardonnay and Pinot Noir; that ranking is not repeated here.

The glass draws on Decanter's 2021 note (lime zest, green apple, pear, maritime), a note of wet chalk and seashells in reviews of other vintages and Boutinot's sheet (nuttiness); the house's winemaker is living and is not named.

records.place: Quebrada Seca, western Limarí Valley; the house at Talagante, Maipo

wine.name: T.H. Chardonnay
wine.sites: A small vineyard at Quebrada Seca, on the western side of the Limarí Valley, nearer the Pacific and its fog than the inland vineyards around Ovalle.
wine.making: Aged about ten months on its lees, in the 2022 vintage mostly in concrete eggs and the rest in used French oak barrels, so the oak stays in the background; the regime moves a little from vintage to vintage.
wine.glass: Lemon, green apple and pear over flint, steely notes and fresh bread, with a touch of hazelnut; piercing acidity and a creamy, salty texture on the finish.
wine.ageing: Lively on release, it fills out over three to five years and should keep for six or so.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white Burgundy glass.

The northern valley of the Coquimbo region around Ovalle, cooled by Pacific fog.

records.table: Undurraga's T.H. Chardonnay is the Limarí wine of an old Maipo house, from Quebrada Seca in the west of the valley near the sea. Aged mostly in concrete eggs, it tastes of lemon, green apple and flint with piercing acidity.
records.story: Undurraga is a Maipo house. Its founder began planning the winery between 1879 and 1883, by the house's own history, and in 1885 founded it at Talagante, south west of Santiago, naming the estate Fundo Santa Ana after his wife; the estate's opening harvest was in 1891, made by a French winemaker. For generations the founding family ran the house. In 2006 the family sold Undurraga, and the new owners invested in vineyards and cellars across Chile. The house's Terroir Hunter range, T.H. on the label, gathers small lots of single varieties from the sites the house judged truest to them, from Leyda to the Limarí. Its Limarí Chardonnay comes from Quebrada Seca, a sector on the western side of the valley, nearer the sea than the vineyards around Ovalle, and Decanter has reviewed it under that name from the 2012 vintage. To a sommelier it is a lesson in how Chile's large houses have come to work: an old Maipo name sending its winemakers north to the fog and lime of the Limarí for a Chardonnay of flint and acidity rather than warmth.

report: The founder is long dead, but his dates were not read in two sources here, so he is described, not named; the house's history page gives his full name.
The sale of 2006 rests on Wine with Seth and South America Wine Guide; the buyers are living and are not named, and the house's present owners are left out as volatile.

The making rests on Uncorked's sheet for the 2022 (ten months, about seven tenths in eggs, the rest in used barrels) and the plan's note of a Brazilian merchant's sheet (ten months in concrete and 500 litre French oak); the house's own sheet was not found, so the vessels are told for 2022 only.
The glass draws on Decanter's 2012 note (flint, steel, fresh bread, citrus, piercing acidity) and the house's own shop sheet (white fruit, hazelnut, creamy and mineral).
Left out for want of a second source: the export to the United States in 1903, the vineyard size and distance from the sea, and the year the Terroir Hunter range began, which one source ties to 2006.

records.place: Los Almendros estate, Limarí Valley; the house at Chimbarongo, Colchagua

wine.name: 20 Barrels Limited Edition Syrah
wine.grapes: Syrah, the great majority, with a little Cabernet Sauvignon and in some vintages a touch of Carmenère.
wine.sites: The house's Los Almendros estate in the Limarí Valley, on poor alluvial and colluvial soils under cloudless skies with very little rain.
wine.making: Aged about sixteen to seventeen months, in the 2017 vintage half in French oak barriques from a single cooperage, half of them new, and half in large foudres, before the blend is made and bottled.
wine.glass: Blackberry, plum and violet over cracked black pepper, clove and a smoky, tarry note; juicy and fresh in the mouth, with a long, meaty finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable after three or four years, it keeps for ten or so from a good vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large Syrah glass.

label.means: The house's selection range, named for the twenty barrels set aside from its 1996 Pinot Noir.
Words the house prints on its 20 Barrels wines to mark a small selection.
The valley of the Coquimbo region around Ovalle, cooled by the Pacific.

records.table: Cono Sur's 20 Barrels Syrah is the Limarí wine of a Colchagua house, from its Los Almendros estate in the north. It tastes of blackberry, violet and cracked pepper with fresh acidity, so pour it beside lamb or a peppered steak.
records.story: Cono Sur, named for the Southern Cone of South America, was created by Concha y Toro in 1993 as a house for new and more adventurous wines, with its cellar at Chimbarongo in the Colchagua Valley. It made its name with Pinot Noir. In 1996 the team set aside twenty barrels of Casablanca Pinot Noir of that year, and the 20 Barrels range was born; the range later grew to wines of several grapes, each from the valley the house judged right for it. For Syrah it looked north, to its Los Almendros estate in the Limarí, and the 20 Barrels Syrah has been listed from that valley in vintages from 2008 onwards. The Limarí suits it: the sun is fierce, but the Pacific and its fog keep the nights cool, and Syrah keeps its pepper and freshness. To a sommelier the wine shows two things at once: a large house choosing a valley for each grape, and the Limarí, known chiefly for Chardonnay, also making a Syrah of perfume and spice.

report: The creation in 1993 by Concha y Toro and the cellar at Chimbarongo rest on Wikipedia and the plan's reading of the parent's own timeline; the present ownership is left out as volatile.
The twenty barrels of 1996 Pinot Noir rest on a wine writer's site and the house's own words quoted on a merchant's page (wine.com); the 20 Barrels Cabernet of 1997 was in one source only and is cut.

The making is the house's 2017 sheet on Bottlebooks (sixteen months, half barriques half new, half foudres); the SAQ gives seventeen months in barrel, so the record says sixteen to seventeen and names no cooper.
The blend is Syrah with a little Cabernet Sauvignon (2017, by the SAQ) and a touch of Carmenère in 2022 (IWSC).
The glass draws on a 2012 tasting note and the International Wine Challenge's notes on 2011 and 2012; the critic of the 2012 note is living and his page is not cited.
Left out for want of a source: the planting year of Los Almendros, its distance from the sea, and the first vintage of the 20 Barrels Syrah, so the story says only that it is listed from 2008.
One competition lists a 2014 20 Barrels Syrah as Maipo; the many other listings give Limarí, so the record keeps Limarí.
